On the second floor of the Rear Hall, there is a shrine dedicated to three emperors who played pivotal roles in establishing the Van Mieu-Quoc Tu Giam and advancing the development of Confucian education in Vietnam: Emperor Ly Thanh Tong (1023-1072), Emperor Ly Nhan Tong (1066-1128), and Emperor Le Thanh Tong (1442-1497).

The architectural splendor of the Thai Hoc buildings is evident in their towering two-story wooden structure, characterized by massive dark-brown wooden columns that support the building’s weight and imbue it with a sense of grandeur. The columns, adorned with moss-covered yin-yang roof tiles, seamlessly blend with the layered curved roof known as mái chồng diêm, which gracefully curves upwards towards the sky.

This distinctive design not only reflects the traditional Vietnamese architectural style but also adds a touch of elegance and solemnity to the overall appearance of the buildings. Surrounded by a spacious red brick courtyard, the Thai Hoc buildings stand out against the backdrop of lush, ancient trees, creating a serene and contemplative environment.
